summary:
ARGUS-1: Night shift on Mars
The best orbital maps of Mars show about 25 cm per pixel, so the rocks that can trip an astronaut in a spacesuit are invisible. And with up to 22 minutes of signal delay, nobody on Earth can drive a rover live to check the ground.
ARGUS-1 gives the robots the night shift. While the crew sleeps, small autonomous rovers drive the route planned for the next day’s walk. They push small rocks off the path, go around rocks that are too big, never touch rocks with scientific value, and mark pits and soft sand to avoid. After every move, one shared map updates itself for every robot and the crew, and a relay satellite would carry it to the base and to Earth. In the morning, the astronaut’s tablet shows a route that was checked on the ground, with before and after photos of each change.
We built a working prototype: a tracked rover with a Raspberry Pi 5, an ESP32, a 3D-printed arm and our own rock detector (3 MB, 19 ms per image, no internet needed). Our site is Airfield Tau in Jezero Crater, where Ingenuity landed before Perseverance arrived. We turned Ingenuity’s photos into a 1 cm per pixel map of the real rocks and combined it with NASA HiRISE imagery, CTX elevation, CRISM minerals, MEDA weather, RAD radiation and DONKI space weather.
The same approach could prepare any crewed walk on Mars or the Moon.
details:
What it does and how it works

The best orbital maps of Mars have about 25 cm per pixel. A rock the size of a football is one blurry pixel, but for an astronaut walking in a suit and carrying equipment, it can cause a fall. With up to 22 minutes of signal delay, nobody on Earth can drive a rover in real time to check the ground.

ARGUS-1 gives the robots the night shift. While the crew sleeps, small autonomous rovers drive the route planned for the next day’s walk. Every rock they find gets a state: small rocks are pushed off the path, rocks that are too big are marked so the route goes around them, and rocks with scientific value are photographed but never touched. The rovers also mark pits and soft sand to avoid. After every move, one shared map updates itself for every robot and the crew. In the concept, a relay satellite carries that map to the base and to Earth. In the morning, the astronaut’s tablet shows a route that was checked on the ground, with before and after photos of every change.

Our demo site is Airfield Tau in Jezero Crater, where the Ingenuity helicopter landed on flight 62 and the Perseverance rover arrived about two months later. We turned Ingenuity’s photos into a 1 cm per pixel map of the real rocks. Our 100 x 60 cm table represents a 10 x 6 m plot there at 1:10 scale, and every rock on the map has its real Mars latitude and longitude.

Benefits

  • Astronauts walk routes checked on the ground, not guessed from orbit.
  • Robots do the slow, repetitive scouting at night, saving crew time and reducing risk during walks.
  • Science targets are protected: the rover never moves a rock the scientists want to study in place.
  • Every robot and crew member works from the same map, which updates itself after each change.
  • The rovers keep working if the connection drops, which on Mars it will.

Intended impact

We want to show that cheap, 3D-printed rovers could prepare every crewed walk on Mars or the Moon, and that each landing site can have a map that improves overnight. The same idea also fits Earth: inspecting rough ground before people enter it after a disaster.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Hardware: a tracked rover with a Raspberry Pi 5 as its brain, an ESP32 controlling the tracks and arm over Bluetooth LE, a 3D-printed arm and gripper, and a USB webcam. We also have a 1U CubeSat as a model of the relay link.
  • Rover software: Python (FastAPI) on the Pi. The SI never drives: it only looks and suggests, and a simple, predictable program sends the commands to the motors. The ESP32 firmware is written in C++ (PlatformIO).
  • Rock detector: our own YOLO26n model, trained on 3,600 frames from the rover’s camera that we labelled automatically with classic computer vision (OpenCV), then compressed to INT8 ONNX. It is 3 MB and takes 19 ms per image on the Pi, with no internet.
  • Map: Python and OpenCV for the camera tracker and map data (GeoJSON), Leaflet and JavaScript for the web map and the astronaut’s tablet.
  • Mission Control: voice and text commands with local SI models (Whisper for speech, Gemma through Ollama, Kokoro for the voice).
  • NASA data: MRO HiRISE imagery, CTX elevation (USGS), CRISM minerals, Ingenuity and Perseverance photos and records, MEDA weather, Curiosity RAD radiation and NASA DONKI space weather.
  • Presentation: Slidev for the slides, Three.js for a 3D video built from real Jezero elevation data, Python CAD scripts for the printed parts.

What makes it creative

  • It treats rovers as the crew’s night shift, a new role for them.
  • The map isn’t fixed: it records every change the robots make, including where each rock was before it moved.
  • We follow the same order as the real mission at Airfield Tau: helicopter first, rover second.
  • It’s a working physical prototype, and it runs a real run on a 1:10 copy of a real Mars site.

Factors we considered

  • Safety: the SI never controls the motors directly, and the rover stops if its computer goes silent.
  • Science: some rocks must never be moved, so they get their own protected state.
  • Communication delay and dropped links: the rover finishes its job alone and reports back later.
  • Accessibility: each rock state on the map is shown with a word as well as a colour, so it works for colour-blind users.
  • Honesty: the site and the data layers are real NASA data. The rocks on our table are stand-ins, and we say so.
  • Cost: cheap, printable hardware, so many rovers can share the work.
